data.text: At 5:35am on 11 December 1994, Ramzi Yousef, the lead planner of the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, boarded Philippine Airlines Flight 434 from Manila to Cebu. In the aircraft lavatory he assembled an IED from materials in his toiletry kit, a watch from his wrist, and a detonator smuggled through security in the heel of his shoe. He set the countdown timer for four hours and then concealed the bomb in the life vest pocket under seat 26K. Less than an hour later Yousef deplaned in Cebu. Four hours after Yousef set his timer, the plane was in flight to Tokyo when the IED exploded under the seat of 24-year-old Haruki Ikegami, killing him and injuring ten others. Unknown to Yousef, the 747 had been modified which put seat 26K over the cargo hold instead of the fuel tank. The pilots made an emergency landing at Naha Airport, Okinawa, saving the remaining 272 passengers. The attack was a test run for the Bojinka Plot, a plan to destroy 11 aircraft mid-flight en route to the United States from Asia in January 1995. It also included a plan to assassinate Pope John Paul II on a scheduled trip to Manila as well as hijacking and flying an aircraft into CIA Headquarters. The plot was foiled when Yousef’s computer was discovered in a Manila apartment the conspirators were using as a base of operations after one of them inadvertently caused a small fire with their bomb making materials. That computer contained detailed files on “Oplan Bojinka.” Coincidently, I was flying home from Australia the day the plot was uncovered and distinctly remember the additional security measures immediately put into place as every passenger was searched from head to toe, to include a detailed inspection of shoes and every item in our luggage and carry-ons. Al-Qaeda learned from the failed Bojinka plot. Those lessons would ultimately form the basis for the September 11th attacks less than a decade later.
